From the Cradle of the Nile: Ethiopia’s Sea-Access Ambitions Take Center Stage at Tana 10 minute read By Ashenafi Endale October 31, 2026 Share Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin Email Telegram Copy URL Sitting on the southern shores of Lake Tana—the mystical, sprawling cradle of the Blue Nile—Bahir Dar offers a striking, almost poetic metaphor for the turbulence currently gripping the Horn of Africa and the wider continent. The Nile has long flowed as the lifeblood of East and North African hydropolitics, binding nations together in an inescapable web of shared geography, competing ambitions, and intense historical rivalry. It was precisely within this metaphorical watershed that policymakers, regional leaders, senior military commanders, and prominent researchers gathered for the 12th Edition of the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa. Returning after a hiatus forced by escalating regional conflicts, the 2026 summit convened under the sharp, pragmatic theme dubbed ‘Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation.’ Yet, while official panel sessions wrestled with the high-minded mechanics of continental trade integration, digital imperialism, monetary frameworks, and macroeconomic governance, the dominant pulse of the conference floor belonged to an unyielding national imperative. Ethiopia’s bold, unapologetic push for reliable, sovereign sea access, set against a backdrop of deep continental fragmentation, the ravages of conflict economies in Sudan and the Sahel, and the urgent demand for structural self-reliance. The deep symbolism of the host city itself exerts its own weigh on the debates that unfolded in Bahirdar. Lake Tana is not merely a geographical landmark; it is the origin point of the Blue Nile, a river that sustains millions downstream while fueling a century-old geopolitical contest over water security, sovereignty, and regional hegemony. In this light, hosting a premier security summit dedicated to economic sovereignty and geopolitical transformation on the very banks of the Nile is deeply profound. From The Reporter Magazine Drought Emergency or Seasonal Deficit ? Published on 2026-09-02 By The Reporter Magazine What the Old Developmental State Got Wrong Published on 2026-10-02 By Samson Berhane 25-Year Sentences & Retroactive Laws: Controversial Draft Law Sparks Fears of Growing Authoritarianism in Tigray Published on 2026-06-21 By Yared Nigussie Red Sea Rivalries: What a Shifting Geopolitical Landscape Means for Ethiopia and The Horn Published on 2026-08-31 By Yared Nigussie East Africa’s enduring hydropolitical tension is mirrored by Ethiopia’s modern strategic dilemma. A nation of over 130 million people, locked behind borders drawn by historical compromises, is seeking a permanent economic outlet to the world. This geographic vulnerability forms the crucible in which Ethiopia’s current foreign policy is forged. When PM Abiy Ahmed took the podium to open the summit, he did not shy away from the persisting core structural realities. Urging African states to shape rather than merely adapt to global power shifts, Abiy placed sovereignty at the center of the continental dialogue, declaring that Africa must stop being a passive recipient of external prescriptions and instead author its own destiny. “By combining its capacities and developing solutions suited to its own realities, Africa can strengthen its role in shaping the global order and securing a better future for generations to come,” Abiy noted, stressing that homegrown solutions are non-negotiable for lasting stability. From The Reporter Magazine From Unwilling Investors to Bidding Wars: Ethiopia’s T-Bill Market Turns on Its Head Published on 2026-09-03 By Mahlet Mehdi Washington Has Sent a Sufficient Signal to PM Abiy on Military Operations: Ex-CIA Analyst Published on 2026-09-28 By Bewket Abebe Behind Ethiopia’s Stalled Iron Ore Mining Published on 2026-08-29 By Bewket Abebe Cities as Engines of Growth and Nation-Building: Reframing Urbanization Discourses in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) Published on 2026-09-14 By Mussie Delelegn Arega (PhD) Crucially, anchoring this push for strategic autonomy, Ethiopian leadership articulated the core national doctrine that secure, unfettered access to the sea is an existential necessity for a growing population of over 130 million, rather than a negotiable diplomatic luxury or a casual geopolitical preference. That message was echoed with striking, unvarnished directness by Ethiopia’s top security and defense leadership. Redwan Hussein, director general of Information Network Security Administration (INSA) and Field Marshal Berhanu Jula, Chief of Staff of Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), underscored during the deliberations that Ethiopia’s national interest in maritime access, framing it not as an aggressive encroachment on neighbors, but as a vital economic lifeline required to prevent structural strangulation and ensure long-term regional stability. However, behind closed doors, in the academic corridors, and among international policy observers, this rhetoric met with analytical scrutiny. Regional and international scholars immediately posed the hard, skeptical question of whether Ethiopian officials are simply staking out a long-term bargaining position to secure alternative port arrangements in a volatile neighborhood, or if there is a tangible, realistic, and peaceful roadmap on the table. Critics note that while the rallying national agenda of maritime rights galvanizes domestic political consensus, navigating the hostile geopolitical realignments of the Red Sea basin demands far more than political will. With the Horn of Africa caught in a web of shifting alliances—marked by friction between Asmara, Cairo, Port Sudan, and Mogadishu, alongside mounting Middle Eastern proxy interventions—analysts warn that uncalibrated maritime ambitions risk inflaming already volatile fault lines unless backed by transparent, cooperative diplomatic frameworks. Presenters and researchers also emphasized that maritime access cannot be separated from the broader architecture of regional trust, arguing that any sustainable framework must reconcile Ethiopia’s legitimate economic needs with the sovereignty and security concerns of neighboring littoral states. The urgency of Ethiopia’s national posture played out against the grim, comprehensive diagnosis detailed in the Tana Secretariat’s official State of Peace and Security in Africa Report, which was presented to the delegates by Tana Board Chairperson and former Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama. The report paints a sobering, data-driven picture of a continent grappling with the dangerous regionalization of violence, the institutionalization of conflict economies, and the erosion of multilateral mediation. Nowhere was this regional contagion more pronounced than in the ongoing catastrophe in Sudan. According to the report’s two-phase analysis covering January 2025 to June 2026, the war underwent a qualitative shift following RSF’s capture of El Fasher, cementing the country’s complete territorial and political fragmentation, with the RSF controlling western gold corridors and the Sudanese Armed Forces holding Khartoum and eastern red sea routes. Panelists detailed how the conflict is sustained by the direct and indirect commodification of violence, where illicit gold trade funnels upwards of USD400 million annually into war chests, financing recruitment, weaponry, and the proliferating use of drones. This internal war has inevitably spilled across borders, drawing in Chad, South Sudan, Egypt, Ethiopia, and proximate Gulf powers, transforming the wider region into a theater of competing middle-power rivalries. Mahama himself underscored the human cost of these dynamics, warning the assembly that Africa cannot achieve economic sovereignty while entire populations are displaced and state institutions collapse under the weight of resource-driven civil wars. The summit also turned a critical eye toward the intractable crises in the eastern DRC, where despite diplomatic milestones like the Declaration of Principles and the Washington Accord, fighting between M23 and government forces has deepened humanitarian tragedies, with rare earth mineral extraction fueling regional logistics networks. In Somalia, the complex security transition from ATMIS to AUSSOM in Somalia, combined with domestic friction over constitutional reform and resource distribution, continues to provide fertile ground for Al-Shabaab’s insurgency, resonating across the wider Red Sea space. Further south, the conflict in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique, has mutated into an elusive rural insurgency where local perceptions of economic exclusion around liquefied natural gas projects threaten to re-ignite communal grievances. Accounting for roughly 55 percent of all conflict-related fatalities on the continent, the Sahel remains Africa’s most volatile security theater, where the withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger from ECOWAS to form the Alliance of Sahel States has dismantled regional coordination, creating security vacuums exploited by jihadist groups. Compounding this instability is a profound technological shift in warfare: the proliferation of commercial and military drones by state and non-state actors across at least nine African countries for reconnaissance, explosive attacks, and online propaganda, cheapening the cost of conflict while exponentially increasing civilian casualties. Moving beyond traditional military paradigms, the 2026 Tana Forum dedicated substantial deliberation to the structural economic traps that underpin continental instability, with panelists and working papers arguing forcefully that security cannot be achieved in an economic vacuum. Delegates dissected the enduring legacy of extractive enclave economies, where African nations export critical raw materials while capturing virtually none of the value-addition, processing revenues, or industrial capabilities. This structural dependency, compounded by heavy debt burdens, unfavorable global trade terms, and reliance on third-party currencies for trade settlement, drains foreign reserves and starves domestic productive sectors of credit. Presenters called for a holistic redefinition of resource sovereignty, arguing that true sovereignty requires exercising total agency across the entire financial and industrial circuit, from local mineral processing and transparent resource-backed lending to domestic invoicing and strengthening intra-African trade channels anchored by the African Continental Free Trade Area. Parallel sessions on the continent’s severe energy deficit, where roughly 600 million Africans still lack reliable electricity, emphasized that regional power integration and transboundary energy pools are indispensable prerequisites for industrialization and sustainable peace. In an era where geopolitical competition has migrated into cyberspace, the forum issued sharp warnings regarding Africa’s digital vulnerability, stressing that digitalization cannot be treated merely as a matter of basic connectivity or technological modernization. When data ecosystems, cloud systems, algorithms, and artificial intelligence are owned and governed externally, African economies risk falling into a modern trap of digital imperialism, prompting experts to demand that African institutions build domestic capabilities in data governance, computing infrastructure, algorithmic transparency, and local software authorship to foster genuine economic independence. Another core pillar of the summit was the complex intersection between regional integration, informal markets, and transnational illicit economies. While the African Union champions regional integration as a vital economic and peace-building tool, the forum acknowledged that formal trade policies alone cannot overcome the realities on the ground, given that a massive share of Africa’s employment and economic activity occurs within the informal sector, functioning as a vital form of bottom-up integration that sustains vulnerable populations across porous borders. However, a critical analytical distinction was drawn between benign informality and destructive illicit economies, noting that while informal cross-border trade provides essential livelihoods, transnational illicit networks, including arms trafficking, environmental plunder, and large-scale trade mis-invoicing by corporate actors, actively fund armed insurgencies and undermine state authority. Empirical papers presented at the forum demonstrated that illicit financial flows are highly adaptive, persisting across fiscal years through entrenched institutional networks, leading delegates to conclude that security and economic integration must go hand in hand, replacing enforcement-only crackdowns with gradual formalization, stronger customs oversight, and the dismantling of high-level illicit financial circuits. As the three-day summit drew to its conclusion, delegates confronted the ultimate, recurring question that haunts high-level diplomatic convenings regarding whether the recommendations emerging from the Tana Forum are legally binding policy mandates or merely an elite agenda-setting platform. The institutional reality is clear. The Tana Forum possesses no direct enforcement mechanism, and its true power lies in its unique, informal character modeled after the traditional African baobab tree, serving as a candid intellectual incubator where sitting leaders, former heads of state, civil society actors, and researchers can speak frankly outside rigid diplomatic protocols. Yet, as Tana Board Chairperson and former Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama bluntly warned in his powerful closing address, the era of endless dialogue must yield to concrete implementation if the forum is to retain its credibility, asserting that it is good to talk and dialogue, but far better to act. Concluding the summit with a direct appeal for continental transformation, Mahama urged leaders “Let us return to Bahirdar next year and say that the tide is turning for Africa, that our conflicts are ending, and opportunities are being created for all our people.” To transform continental agency from a political slogan into tangible reality, the forum’s final recommendations mapped out a rigorous path forward, including granting Regional Economic Communities predictable and multi-year institutional funding rather than leaving them at the mercy of short-term donor whims when deploying peace support operations. Presenters also emphasized the necessity of institutionalizing public accountability by establishing transparent tracking mechanisms, such as public publication of treaty-ratification statuses, independent performance assessments of early-warning systems, and granting parliaments and media access to continental security data to ensure governments honor their commitments. Furthermore, researchers and panelists stressed the urgency of bridging the dangerous gap between detecting security risks and mobilizing rapid institutional responses before local disputes cascade into full-scale regional wars, while ensuring that formal peace agreements integrate economic restructuring, equitable resource-sharing, and local benefit thresholds to make peace structurally more profitable than war for conflict protagonists. Backdropped by the eternal, life-giving flow of the Blue Nile in Bahirdar, the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa delivered a stark, uncompromising message. Whether confronting Ethiopia’s bold geopolitical push for maritime access, managing the devastating resource-driven fragmentation of Sudan and the Sahel, or building robust economic and digital sovereignty, Africa’s path to sustainable peace requires moving past rhetorical posturing into disciplined, unified action. The intellectual framework has been laid bare by scholars, leaders, and security chiefs alike, and whether African governance structures possess the political discipline and institutional courage to translate these recommendations into hard policy remains the ultimate, defining test for the continent’s future. Drawing on the Forum recommendations, mainstreaming and working on the implementation part; takes African governments, international partners, regional and continental organizations renewing their commitments, actionable plans. When a country’s geographic bottleneck is policed by a deeply militarized dictator with no clear economic vision, the resulting friction transcends ordinary bilateral disputes, elevating infrastructure into a primary casus belli. No regional dynamic illustrates this geopolitical chokehold more acutely than the volatile relationship between Ethiopia and Eritrea. For decades, international observers have viewed Ethiopia’s quest for a seaport through a purely commercial lens, equating it as a matter of trade balances, shipping tariffs, and economic optimization. But as the Red Sea rapidly transforms into one of the most volatile, hyper-militarized maritime corridors on the planet, this perspective is dangerously obsolete. For Ethiopia, a nation of over 130 million people, permanent and reliable access to the sea is no longer just an economic aspiration. It is an existential imperative for national security and survival. This assertion makes sense if viewed critically beyond a shallow attempt to reduce the looming danger to a simple expansionist ambition. One must always reconsider the facts on the ground while analyzing the conundrum in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia, a country that is only 60 kms from the Red sea, is the most populous landlocked country in the world, whose significant portion of the population is youth and in active pursuit of job opportunities. According to recent IMF reports, the country is also home to the fastest growing economy in the entire sub-Saharan Africa. This is not merely a statistical trivia point framed for political purpose; rather it is a profound strategic vulnerability. Every piece of medicine, fuel, and technology that enters the country, and every single product exported to sustain its economy, depends entirely on the political whims and stability of its coastal neighbors. Currently, Ethiopia relies on Djibouti for roughly 95% of its trade, paying upwards between $1.5 to $2 billion annually in port fees. This single door dependency is an economic chokehold. No sovereign state can safely anchor its future on a single corridor that is vulnerable to external influences. For countries like Ethiopia, the highly volatile security situation in its surrounding doubles down the impact, without mentioning the challenges associated with the growing number of military bases in the region. Should political instability or hostile foreign influence freeze the docks of Djibouti, the Ethiopian economy would collapse triggering an internal humanitarian catastrophe of unprecedented scale. This is what makes Ethiopia’s concern undeniably legitimate and fuels its determination to address what it perceives as an existential threat through any means available. Just as a drowning person instinctively tries every possible option to stay afloat. A nation of 130 million people cannot be trapped in a geographic cage at the mercy of volatile, highly militarized autocratic coastal regime. A stable, secure Horn of Africa is impossible if its largest engine of population and economic powerhouse is kept in a state of permanent anxiety and artificial suffocation. Securing a permanent and dependable commercial and naval gateway to the Red Sea is not an empire building ambition or a luxury. For Ethiopia, it is becoming a simple, legitimate right to breath and it is the only way to bring peace and security in the entire Horn. Encirclement, Exclusion, and Ethiopia’s Security Imperative The urgency underpinning Ethiopia’s vulnerability has been sharply accelerated by the growing securitization of the Red Sea. What was once an open global trade route has become an arena for geopolitical chess, dominated by state coalitions and non-state actors from near and afar. Global and regional powers increasingly framing the vital corridor as a critical national security priority rather than just a commercial shipping lane. Driven by the need to safeguard chokepoints like the Bab el Mandab Strait from asymmetric threats, piracy, and regional conflicts, world powers have rapidly expanded their footprint through a dense concentration of military bases along the coastline. Djibouti has become the primary epicenter of this militarization, uniquely hosting overlapping naval facilities for both the United States (Camp Lemonnier) and China, alongside presence from France and Japan. Concurrently, nations like Russia have sought access, while regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkye, and Israel are all vying for influence via port logistics and security pacts along the broader Horn of Africa. While these external militaries provide short-term protection for international shipping, their crowding presence has ultimately transformed the Red Sea into a complex arena of overlapping geopolitical rivalries and proxy vulnerabilities, weakening the prospects for a self-sustaining regional security framework and brutally doubling down on Ethiopia’s unique vulnerability. As if these threats are not enough, Ethiopia is alarmed by a recent development of an architectural web of alliances orchestrated explicitly to isolate it from its own geographic backyard. The creation of the El Alamein Joint Declaration by Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia is not as a routine diplomatic pact, but a deliberate strategy of encirclement. By codifying that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states, regional adversaries seek to permanently deny landlocked Ethiopia a seat at the table. Proofing that the danger felt by Ethiopia is eminent beyond perception and this could potentially leave the country to consider every option to break the chokehold before it is too late. The action Ethiopia should take would be determined based on the scale and level of threats the country is faced with, as the end justifies the means. This encirclement is amplified by Egypt’s aggressive forward deployment rhetoric in the region. Driven by tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Cairo is trying to weaponize Ethiopia’s landlocked status by forming tight military and logistical alliances with Eritrea and other states bordering Ethiopia. From the Ethiopian perspective, it is quite clear. Hostile foreign militaries are aspiring to setting up base camps right on its borders, holding the keys to the very maritime gates that feed the Ethiopian population. This is a recuring dangerous move. Previously, when multinational coalitions form to protect Red Sea shipping lines from asymmetric threats like piracy and militant groups, Ethiopia is routinely excluded. Addis Ababa is being forced to watch from the sidelines while its primary economic lifeblood is policed by an alliance sympathetic to its rivals. It is profoundly naïve to expect Ethiopia to remain passive while such a perilous scheme is being orchestrated to threaten the lives of its entire population and its very survival. This reality underscores Ethiopia’s existential need to secure a reliable maritime corridor through which it can establish dependable port services and maintain a sovereign naval capability. Such a capability is essential to safeguard its national interests, protect its flag-bearing vessels, and guarantee its unhindered right to innocent passage under international law. Ethiopia has consistently expressed its preference for cooperation and has repeatedly advanced frameworks centered on mutual economic integration, shared prosperity, and regional interdependence. However, while Ethiopia remains committed to peaceful collaboration, coastal states, particularly Eritrea, should recognize that legal technicalities or strategies aimed at regional containment cannot serve as sustainable solutions to a matter that directly concerns the livelihood, security, and future of such burgeoning population. When the survival and long-term interests of the entire nation is at stake, it is unrealistic to expect Ethiopia to remain passive. It will undoubtedly pursue all the necessary strategic measures to secure its legitimate access to the Red Sea and protect its vital national interests. In doing so, it will ensure that its sovereignty, security, and economic future are safeguarded both on land and at sea. In conclusion, Ethiopia’s demand for access to the sea must be understood by its neighbouring countries as a legitimate strategic and economic and security concerns that deserves serious, constructive, and peaceful consideration. Why would Ethiopia’s quest to establish a military base along the Red Sea coast be considered unacceptable when countries from far beyond the region already maintain military bases and enjoy strategic access to the same coastline? Is it just to deny a neighbouring country with vital security and economic interests in the region an opportunity to negotiate such access, while external powers are permitted to establish a military presence there? The issue should not be approached through double standards or geopolitical rivalries, but through constructive dialogue, mutual respect, and negotiated arrangements that uphold the sovereignty of coastal states while addressing Ethiopia’s legitimate interests. IGAD and the African Union must urgently take their leadership responsibilities by facilitating inclusive regional dialogue and developing a practical framework that addresses Ethiopia’s legitimate aspirations while safeguarding the legitimate interests of neighbouring states. External actors outside the Horn of Africa should be discouraged from pursuing their agendas by fostering hostility and division, rather than promoting cooperation, dialogue, and regional stability. The international community, including the United Nations and other influential partners, should also intensify diplomatic engagement and support a negotiated settlement before the situation deteriorates into a dangerous confrontation with far reaching consequences for the Horn of Africa and beyond. The time to act is now: through timely diplomacy, mutual understanding, and political courage, regional leaders and international stakeholders can transform a potential source of conflict into an opportunity for cooperation, shared prosperity, and lasting peace. Failure to act decisively today risks allowing tensions to spiral into a devastating conflict that the region and the wider world can ill afford. What next? Wikimedia Commons A false-color image of the area surrounding the coastal city of Assab and the Red Sea coast, based on satellite imagery data captured on 23 October 2019. The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war Amgad Fareid Eltayeb last update on 30 Oct 2026 The dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea over the Red Sea port of Assab now extends well beyond that of a maritime facility or outlet for international trade. It reflects a structural contradiction between two states with a shared history but divided on issues like sovereignty, security, borders, and the state itself. For Ethiopia, Assab embodies its historical loss of direct access to the sea. This is a growing strategic concern, with the country’s population and economy both having expanded. For Eritrea, the port is a key and inseparable part of its sovereignty, won through a long war of independence. Thus, the port mixes economic interests with domestic power struggles, regional alliances, and foreign intervention, particularly in a region already afflicted by weak state institutions and protracted armed conflicts. The modern roots of the crisis lie in Italian colonial expansion in the 19th century. Italian control of Assab began in 1869 through the Rubattino shipping company, which acquired the right to administer the port from local authorities. Administration passed to the Italian state in 1882, and Assab subsequently became part of Italian Eritrea, formally established as a colony in 1890. With the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, this was a time of intensifying European competition for ports and trade routes through the Red Sea. Italy lost control of East Africa in 1941, when Assab and the rest of Eritrea came under British occupation and administration. Following the Second World War, Eritrea’s future administration was debated. On 2 December 1950, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 390, recommending the establishment of a federation between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The arrangement came into effect in 1952. It recognised Ethiopia’s legitimate need for access to the sea, and granted autonomy to Eritrea (with its own legislative, executive and judicial institutions responsible for internal affairs) within a federation under the sovereignty of the Ethiopian Crown. The resolution did not grant Ethiopia permanent ownership of Assab as a separate sovereign possession, but it went beyond a commercial agreement between two independent states by establishing a federation with sovereign authority at the federal level, defined powers, and Eritrean autonomy. These legal distinctions remain essential to assessing the competing claims surrounding Assab today. Emperor Haile Selassie gradually undermined Eritrea’s autonomous institutions before abolishing the federal system and fully annexing the territory in 1962. A year earlier, Eritrea’s armed struggle for independence had already begun. The Ethiopian Empire fell in the revolution of 1974, and the military regime of Mengistu Haile Mariam reasserted centralised control through force. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters arrive after eight hours of walking in Mekele, the capital of the Tigray region, Ethiopia, on 29 June 2021. Alliances and interests Opposition to his rule fostered cooperation between the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front (EPLF) and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which was waging a parallel campaign to overthrow the regime. Their common struggle contributed to Mengistu’s defeat in 1991, although the alliance concealed a fundamental difference between their political ambitions: the Eritrean movement sought to establish an independent state, while the Tigrayan movement aimed to overthrow the regime and restructure power within Ethiopia. A common enemy had united them, but victory exposed their conflicting visions of statehood. Eritrea gained independence in 1993 following a popular referendum endorsed by Ethiopia’s new government, then led by Meles Zenawi, and it was recognised by the international community. Independence made Ethiopia landlocked, losing its direct access to the Red Sea. Yet this did not disappear overnight. The country continued to use Assab under arrangements agreed with Eritrea, until mounting economic, territorial and political disputes culminated in the 1998–2000 war. This ended with the Algiers Agreement, followed by the boundary commission’s ruling in 2002. Relations between the two countries remained hostile and Ethiopia shifted almost all its maritime trade to Djibouti. Subsequent demographic and economic developments have sharpened the consequences. Ethiopia now has 135 million people, a growing industrial economy, and a thirst for international trade, but with almost all its foreign trade passing through Djibouti, it depends heavily on a single transit route. That dependence creates genuine economic vulnerabilities. Sign up for our Weekly Newsletter Get the best of Majalla, straight to your inbox. Ethiopia has 135 million people, a growing industrial base, and a thirst for international trade, but almost all trade depends on a single transit route through Djibouti 'Existential necessity' It is not surprising that a country of Ethiopia's size should want to diversify its maritime outlets and secure reliable access to global markets, but however legitimate its economic needs may be, they confer no sovereign entitlement to another country's territory. The right of access to the sea is fundamentally different from the right to a coastline, just as facilitating trade is distinct from redrawing borders. Since October 2023, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has increasingly presented access to the Red Sea as an existential necessity, bound up with the country's future and security. His rhetoric has extended beyond improving commercial transit arrangements to demands for sovereign maritime access and naval capabilities. He invoked history to portray the loss of Ethiopia's coastline as a historical wrong that now needed to be corrected. This rhetoric has coincided with severe domestic crises, particularly in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with local authorities in Somaliland, a coastal region of Somalia that wants to break away. The proposed arrangement envisaged a stretch of coastline and the establishment of a naval facility in exchange for Ethiopian recognition of Somaliland's independence. Somalia's federal government rejected the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, triggering tensions. Mediation by Türkiye produced the Ankara Declaration in December 2024, which acknowledged the possibility of Ethiopia securing sustainable commercial access to the sea under Somali sovereignty, without granting it a sovereign coastal outlet. In December 2025, Israel (which also wants Red Sea access) became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland. Ethiopia's attempt to obtain sovereign maritime access through the Somali coast stalled, which brought renewed attention to the port of Assab, which occupies a distinctive place in Ethiopia's political memory. Somaliland President Abdirahman Abdullahi Mohamed during a press conference with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar at the Presidential Palace in Hargeisa, 6 January 2026. Collapsing rapprochement The rapprochement between Ethiopia and Eritrea that began in 2018 was now collapsing. The reconciliation between Addis Ababa and Asmara had developed into a military alliance against the TPLF during the 2020-22 war, but the Pretoria Agreement, which ended that conflict, was subsequently signed without Eritrea's participation, creating a deep rift between the two countries. With no lasting framework for shared economic interests and mutual security guarantees, relations depended on a convergence of interests and calculations regarding domestic adversaries. As the arrangements underpinning Pretoria unravelled, Eritrea developed ties to the TPLF, despite them having fought so bitterly just a few years earlier. In September 2026, large-scale fighting resumed in Tigray. Ethiopian soldiers advanced, capturing Mekelle, the regional capital, before moving towards the Eritrean border. Thus began the latest and most dangerous phase. Addis Ababa and Asmara severed diplomatic relations and accused each other of military interference, support for armed groups, and aggression. Ethiopia invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter to justify measures it said it was taking in self-defence. Eritrea accused Ethiopia of using these claims as a pretext for seizing Assab. Military movements and mounting threats on both sides have now heightened the risk of war. This escalation cannot be understood in isolation. Foreign states have an interest in the Horn of Africa and seek to exploit state weaknesses. Ethiopia maintains close ties with the United Arab Emirates, which has economic and military influence in the ports of the region and across regional supply networks. Israel's recognition of Somaliland also signalled support for Ethiopia's ambitions to secure maritime access there. For Sudan, which has been ravaged by an ongoing civil war, the prospect of fighting between Ethiopia and Eritrea poses a direct threat. The Sudanese Armed Forces are fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which now controls the giant Darfur region in western Sudan. The RSF supply network is said to include the UAE, but Abu Dhabi denies it. The International Crisis Group cites reports that RSF forces are stationed in the Benishangul-Gumuz region near the border and launch attacks from there into Sudan's Blue Nile region. Should war break out, the militarisation of the border, the flow of weapons and fighters, and further waves of displacement would compound these dangers, adding to the burden on Sudan. Any Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore draw in overlapping conflicts and foreign actors. The harbour of Port Sudan on the Red Sea on 24 February 2014. It is Sudan's main seaport and source of 90% of its international trade. Dangers of escalation The maritime trade routes around the Horn of Africa are some of the world's busiest and most sensitive, as they intersect with the strategic interests of regional and global powers. Any extension of hostilities towards Eritrea's coastline would increase the risks to ports and shipping, drive up transport and insurance costs, and add more instability in a maritime corridor already suffering the repercussions of the civil war in Yemen. The African Union has a particular responsibility to turn its calls for restraint into urgent diplomatic action. It could reopen communication channels between Addis Ababa and Asmara, establish verifiable arrangements to prevent military clashes along the border, and support the resumption of a political process to address the conflict in Tigray. Regional governments could likewise approach the crisis as a shared threat to stability, rather than an opportunity to alter the balance of power in their favour. Saudi Arabia and Türkiye could help reduce tensions, forge understandings, and safeguard security in the Red Sea, but foreign powers supplying weapons must also commit to ending any military and financial assistance that fuels confrontation. Some call for peace while supplying the means to wage war. There is no inherent legal conflict between Ethiopia's right of access to the sea and Eritrea's sovereignty over its territory. International law recognises the legitimate interests and transit rights of landlocked states, while granting them no right to seize the territory of coastal countries. Respect for borders inherited at independence remains a cornerstone of the African regional order. Together with the prohibition on the use of force enshrined in the UN Charter, this principle places clear limits on territorial claims. A boatman transports visitors along a shore near the old port of Massawa—located 60 kilometers from the Eritrean capital—including civilians arriving from Ethiopia to visit Eritrea's Dahlak Islands. Contractual agreements, joint investments, and reciprocal security arrangements could provide practical solutions to the question of maritime access without reopening disputes over sovereignty. Ethiopia and Eritrea have already demonstrated that Eritrean independence can coexist with Ethiopian use of the port of Assab. Geography did not end that arrangement; it collapsed because political and security understandings between the two countries broke down. Renewing cooperation will require more than another port agreement; it will demand measures to address mutual security concerns, backed by international guarantees. A region at stake Assab represents a test of the future political and security order in the Horn of Africa, with implications far beyond the fate of a port. Ethiopia's need for maritime access is an economic and strategic reality, but turning that need into a claim to sovereignty is no remedy for the underlying economic problem and threatens to ignite a fresh dispute over borders and legitimacy. For Eritrea, defending independence and sovereignty is compatible with establishing good economic relations with its larger neighbour. For the countries of the Horn of Africa, not least Sudan, preventing war is essential to protecting their own security and sovereignty. In a region exhausted by conflict and the collapse of state institutions, the greatest danger is that an attempt to change Ethiopia's landlocked status by force ignites another war, at a cost to all concerned far greater than any benefit its proponents hope to gain. + / - SAVE SHARE Related topics Tigray Ethiopia Eritrea Red Sea Port international trade Horn of Africa Sudan Related Articles The leaders of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea met in Alamein Egypt on 4 October to discuss regional tensions. Civilian accounts from the Amhara, Oromia, Wolaita, and Southwest Ethiopia regions detail a pattern of forced recruitment, arbitrary street detentions, and enforced disappearances. Security forces and kebele militias systematically target young men in urban centers, transit hubs, and rural districts—particularly individuals unable to produce state identity documents. Witnesses report that recruitment operations frequently occur after dusk or in public gathering spaces, including football venues, coffee stalls, and roadside checkpoints, with victims loaded onto military buses and transported to undisclosed holding facilities or training camps. In Sodo within the Wolaita Zone, as well as across districts in South Wollo and Debre Birhan, residents report self-imposed curfews and severe restrictions on daily movement to evade patrol units. Witnesses in Southeast Arsi’s Lude Hetosa woreda described forced sweeps where minors under 18, orphans, and migrant daily laborers were rounded up to fulfill local kebele recruitment quotas without family notification or formal administrative review. While ground sources in Mizan Aman and Wolaita note that public outcry and media scrutiny have led to a temporary decrease in sweep operations in select localities, fear remains pervasive among youth, who describe the recruitment as effectively irreversible disappearance. Anonymous defense personnel acknowledged ongoing recruitment activities but claimed no central government order had been issued for forced conscription. Defense attorneys and human rights monitors emphasize that forced street roundups bypass statutory military recruitment standards and violate constitutional protections against arbitrary detention. __ Join our Telegram Channel : t.me/borkena Like borkena on Facebook Ethiopian Sports News Join the conversation. ethiopia.summary: Young men across Ethiopia are experiencing heightened anxiety due to widespread forced conscription drives conducted by local militias and security forces. Reports from regions such as Amhara, Oromia, Wolaita, and Southwest Ethiopia highlight a disturbing pattern of arbitrary street detentions and enforced disappearances targeting individuals, particularly those without state identity documents. Recruitment operations often occur in public spaces after dark, with victims being forcibly taken to undisclosed military facilities. Residents in areas like Sodo and South Wollo have resorted to self-imposed curfews to avoid these patrols. Disturbingly, minors and vulnerable individuals, including orphans and migrant laborers, are also being rounded up to meet local recruitment quotas without any formal notification to families. While some public outcry has temporarily reduced the frequency of these operations, fear remains pervasive among the youth, who view the conscription as a form of irreversible disappearance. The closing ceremony was attended by HE Ambassador of the State of Qatar to the Federal Republic of Somalia Dr. Abdullah bin Salem Al Nuaimi. The campaign provided medical examinations and diagnostic assessments for 144 children with heart conditions and congenital heart defects. A total of 40 cardiac catheterization procedures were performed on children whose conditions required specialized treatment, under the supervision of a team of consultants and specialists in pediatric cardiology and cardiac catheterization. Speaking at the closing ceremony, Director of Qatar Charity's Somalia Office Abdulfattah Adam Moallim said the campaign had exceeded its target of treating 35 cases by performing 40 cardiac catheterization procedures for children. This was a direct response to growing medical needs. He also announced that Qatar Charity is preparing to launch a specialized campaign for pediatric open-heart surgery before the end of the year. The campaign will address cases requiring advanced surgical interventions whose treatment needs could not be met through cardiac catheterization and heart defect repair campaigns. Partners and Doctors described the campaign's success as a significant medical and humanitarian achievement, with Consultant in Pediatric Congenital Cardiology and Cardiac Catheterization at the Mogadishu Heart Center and Dean of the Faculty of Medicine and Surgery at Mogadishu University Dr. Mohamed Ahmed Mohamed affirming that the campaign's results had given dozens of children a new chance at life and a more hopeful future. Consultant in Pediatric Cardiology and Cardiac Catheterization Dr. Iyad Al-Amouri praised the trust placed in the medical team by Somali families and the considerable efforts of young Somali medical professionals, whom he described as an important asset for the future of the country's health sector. Qatar Charity previously carried out three specialized campaigns in Somalia to treat heart defects and conditions in children, benefiting 97 boys and girls. With the 40 cardiac catheterization procedures performed during the current campaign, the total number of children benefiting from therapeutic procedures and cardiac catheterization has risen to 137. Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Mawisley militias abandon front lines in central Somalia Mawisley militias abandon front lines in central Somalia November 1, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Hawadle clan militias that fought Al Shabaab alongside government forces have abandoned front-line positions in Somalia’s central Hiran region, Caasimada Online news website reported on Sunday, as clan leaders push to form an administration independent of the federal government. The fighters, known as Macawisley, have left posts in the Mataban and Buulo Barde districts, and there are fears they could also quit Jalalaqsi town. Clan fighters seized control of the regional capital, Beledweyne, over the weekend, taking over the provincial headquarters and other government offices. About 2,000 heavily armed clan fighters are now in the town as part of a plan by Hawadle political figures to create an authority separate from Mogadishu and from Hirshabelle, the federal member state that includes Hiran. Fears of further defections There are concerns that Hawadle soldiers serving in the federal army in Hiran could also defect, a move that would leave the remaining government-held areas exposed to Al Shabaab. The insurgent group has retaken much of the ground gained by the militias and the army in 2022 and 2023, after a major counter-offensive in 2025. The Macawisley were formed in 2022 to fight Al Shabaab and received support from the federal government, Ethiopia and the United States. Abdullahi Mohamed Ali Sanbalolshe, a former head of the National Intelligence and Security Agency, said recently that they planned to set up an administration to confront the government in Hiran. He said it would ally with anyone, including Al Shabaab, to remove President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. Dispute over Hirshabelle leadership Hawadle politicians say Mohamud promised their clan the Hirshabelle presidency, then reneged and sidelined them. They accuse the federal government of backing incumbent regional president Ali Gudlawe in a re-election vote that Mogadishu organised and whose outcome it controlled. It is unclear how the standoff will end or whether Mogadishu will send reinforcements to Hiran region. The departure leaves Somalia without an agreed international mechanism to help resolve a dispute over whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and parliament can remain in office until 2027. The government says constitutional amendments provide a legal basis for the extended terms. Opposition leaders reject that interpretation. The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia, known as UNTMIS, formally concluded its operations after a two-year transition intended to transfer its responsibilities to Somali institutions and other UN agencies. The closure marks the end of a succession of UN political missions that began in the early 1990s, following the collapse of Somalia’s central government. Over the years, those missions helped convene negotiations among rival leaders, facilitated agreements on power-sharing and supported efforts to resolve election disputes. Their involvement did not eliminate Somalia’s recurring political crises, but it provided a channel through which competing factions could negotiate, often with international assistance. No comparable mediation framework has been established to replace that role, according to Al Jazeera, leaving the government and opposition to seek a settlement through direct negotiations. The federal government maintains that constitutional amendments adopted under Mohamud’s administration allow the president and members of parliament to remain in office until 2027. Opposition groups dispute that position, arguing against extending the current leadership’s tenure. Mohamud has invited opposition figures to talks aimed at resolving the dispute, but major opposition groups have not confirmed whether they will participate. The mission’s closure followed a request by the Somali government in 2024 to end the UN’s direct political role in the country. Government officials had accused the organisation of interfering in domestic affairs and sought greater Somali responsibility for political and institutional matters. The transition gradually transferred the mission’s responsibilities to national institutions and other parts of the UN system. The withdrawal does not end the UN’s presence in Somalia. Its humanitarian and development agencies will continue operating, although their mandates do not include the political mediation previously undertaken by the mission. Neither the government nor the opposition has announced an agreed procedure for resolving the constitutional dispute, and no alternative mediator has been formally designated if direct negotiations fail. Major opposition groups have yet to confirm whether they will accept Mohamud’s invitation to talks on the constitutional dispute and election timetable. The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) ceased operations on Saturday after completing a two-year transition requested by the Somali government, the mission said in a statement on X. Its responsibilities have been gradually transferred to Somali institutions, UN agencies and the UN office supporting African Union (AU) troops under a roadmap agreed between Somalia and the UN. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Somalia’s progress but called for continued international backing amid political, security and humanitarian challenges. Strained relations The closure follows years of sometimes strained relations between Somali governments and the UN mission, whose involvement in domestic politics has repeatedly prompted accusations of interference. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s government formally requested its withdrawal in 2024. At a farewell ceremony in Mogadishu on Monday, Deputy Prime Minister Saleh Ahmed Jama hailed the closure as a “day of victory”, saying Somalia was now leaving behind the “era of transition”. The departure comes as international support for Somalia is shrinking, even as the country faces deep political divisions and continuing violence. Opposition leaders reject the government’s position that constitutional changes allow President Mohamud and parliament to remain in office until 2027. Relations with some regional leaders are also strained, while al-Shabab , an armed group linked to al-Qaeda, continues to fight government forces. The UN mission previously helped rival leaders reach election agreements, but no replacement for its mediation role has been agreed. Mohamud has invited political opponents to talks, although major opposition groups have yet to confirm their attendance. UN humanitarian and development agencies remain in Somalia, but their funding has been hard-hit by cuts to international aid. In August, the UN children’s agency said 205 health and nutrition facilities had closed because of aid cuts. AU troops also remain to support Somali forces against al-Shabab, but their operations depend heavily on a separate UN office, UNSOS, providing food, fuel, medical care and transport. However, that vital support could end by December 2027 under a US-backed plan to close the UN office providing it, the Reuters news agency reported in September. somalia.content: Somalia Gains Duty-Free Access to EU Market Under Trade Scheme - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Gains Duty-Free Access to EU Market Under Trade Scheme Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 1, 2026 Brussels (HOL) — Somali producers are eligible to sell qualifying goods in European Union markets without paying import duties or facing export-volume quotas, under a preferential trade arrangement that could help local businesses expand their overseas sales. The arrangement gives Somali exporters a potential cost advantage when competing in European markets, but businesses must still meet EU product standards and import requirements before their goods can enter the bloc. The EU Delegation to Somalia said in a social media statement that Somalia is among 33 African countries benefiting from the Everything But Arms (EBA) initiative, which provides duty-free and quota-free market access to countries classified among the world's least developed economies. The scheme covers eligible products except arms and ammunition, allowing qualifying shipments to enter EU markets without customs duties or restrictions on the quantity exported under the arrangement. For Somali businesses seeking customers abroad, the preferential terms remove two trade barriers that can make exporting more expensive or limit the volume of goods entering foreign markets. The EU Delegation said the arrangement has no fixed expiry date, offering businesses a continuing opportunity to develop export operations and seek customers in Europe. However, the announcement does not represent a newly negotiated trade agreement or an immediate increase in Somali exports. Somalia's access falls under an existing EU trade preference scheme. Export opportunities depend on meeting EU standards Although the arrangement removes tariffs and quotas, Somali producers must still comply with European quality standards and other import regulations. Those requirements remain a major consideration for businesses assessing whether they can sell their products competitively in the European market. Exporters that satisfy the standards could benefit from reduced trade costs and access to customers without the additional burden of EU import duties on qualifying goods. The absence of quotas also means eligible exporters would not face a fixed limit on shipment volumes under the scheme. The EU Delegation presented the arrangement as an opportunity for Somali businesses to expand production and strengthen their presence in international markets. However, any increase in exports would depend on businesses finding buyers, meeting regulatory requirements and developing the capacity to supply European markets. The delegation's statement did not identify particular Somali products expected to benefit, provide figures for existing exports to the EU or estimate how much additional trade the scheme could generate. It also did not announce any new export contracts or investments resulting from the preferential access. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia EU investigates reported hijacking of Iranian fishing vessel off Somalia Posted by: Horseed Staff The European Union’s naval mission is investigating the reported hijacking of an Iranian fishing vessel off north-eastern Somalia, amid renewed concerns over the security of commercial shipping in the region. 1 November, 2026 Share Tweet The Maritime Security Centre–Indian Ocean (MSCIO), which supports the EU’s Operation ATALANTA, said the fishing vessel Azini was reportedly hijacked at about 09:00 UTC on 29 October. In an update issued on 31 October, the MSCIO said the vessel was approaching a maritime traffic lane and could potentially be used as a “mothership” to support further piracy operations. The warning does not establish that the Azini has been used to launch attacks. The condition and whereabouts of its crew remain unclear, while authorities have not identified those responsible for the reported hijacking. The vessel’s reported movement towards a shipping lane has nevertheless raised concerns about the potential risk to merchant ships operating off Somalia’s north-eastern coast. Fishing vessels can potentially be used by pirate groups as motherships, allowing them to operate farther from the coast and providing a platform from which smaller boats can be deployed. Such a development could widen the area in which commercial vessels face a potential piracy threat. Initial information indicates that the Azini held a fishing licence issued by Puntland authorities and was represented by a businessman from the semi-autonomous Somali region. However, Horseed Media reported that it had been unable to independently verify those additional details. The reported hijacking comes amid renewed maritime security activity in Puntland. Puntland maritime forces recently freed three cargo vessels that had been held by suspected pirates off the coast of the region, in the Nugaal, Karkaar and Ras Casayr areas. The latest incident is likely to be closely monitored by maritime authorities as they assess whether the reported hijacking could develop into a wider threat to shipping in waters off Somalia. استبدل صلاح بعد مرور 60 دقيقة من مباراة أنغولا ضمن تصفيات كأس أمم أفريقيا 2027، وقال في المؤتمر الصحافي عقب اللقاء إن القرار جاء «لأسباب فنية». وبعدها غادر صلاح المعسكر، وغاب عن المباراة التالية أمام جنوب السودان، وهو ما أوضح مدرب المنتخب أنه تم بالاتفاق مع اللاعب بسبب إقامة المباراة على أرضية من العشب الصناعي حفاظاً على سلامته. كما غاب مهاجم طرابزون سبور عن المباراة الودية أمام جنوب أفريقيا لاحقاً، وسط تساؤلات عديدة بشأن موقفه من الانضمام إلى المعسكر المقبل في نوفمبر. وسعى حسن بعد ذلك إلى احتواء التوتر، مؤكداً احترامه لجميع اللاعبين، وفي مقدمتهم قائد المنتخب صلاح، الذي وصفه بأنه «من أهم اللاعبين في العالم». ويستعد منتخب مصر لخوض مواجهتي مالاوي ضمن الجولتين الثالثة والرابعة من التصفيات المؤهلة إلى كأس أمم أفريقيا 2027، حيث ينطلق المعسكر في التاسع من نوفمبر بمركز المنتخبات الوطنية. ومن المقرر أن يلتقي المنتخبان يوم 13 نوفمبر على استاد القاهرة الدولي ضمن منافسات الجولة الثالثة، قبل أن تتجدد المواجهة بينهما يوم 17 من الشهر نفسه في مالاوي ضمن الجولة الرابعة. ويتصدر منتخب مصر المجموعة الثانية برصيد 4 نقاط، متفوقاً بفارق الأهداف على أنغولا صاحبة المركز الثاني، بينما تحتل مالاوي المركز الثالث برصيد 3 نقاط، ويقبع منتخب جنوب السودان في المركز الأخير دون رصيد. وكان المنتخب المصري قد استهل مشواره بالتعادل السلبي أمام أنغولا في القاهرة، قبل أن يحقق فوزاً كبيراً على جنوب السودان خارج أرضه بخمسة أهداف دون رد. وقال الاتحاد المصري إن إبراهيم حاجي عثمان أوغلو، رئيس الاتحاد التركي، الفنية والإدارية، وتطوير برامج إعداد المنتخبات الوطنية، إلى جانب التعاون في مجالات التحكيم وتطوير المواهب والبنية المؤسسية لكرة القدم. وشهد اللقاء الاتفاق على إعداد بروتوكول تعاون مشترك بين الاتحادين football.summary: كشف الاتحاد الأفريقي لكرة القدم «كاف» عن مواعيد مباريات الأندية المصرية الزمالك وبيراميدز والأهلي في بطولتي دوري أبطال أفريقيا والكونفدرالية لموسم 2026/2027. حيث سيتنافس الزمالك وبيراميدز في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، بينما يشارك الأهلي في الكونفدرالية. تم تقسيم الفرق إلى أربع مجموعات، حيث وقع الزمالك في المجموعة الثانية مع يانج أفريكانز التنزاني، مولودية الجزائر، والنادي الأفريقي التونسي. تبدأ مباريات الزمالك في الجولة الأولى بمواجهة الأفريقي التونسي في نهاية نوفمبر 2026. من جهة أخرى، يلعب بيراميدز في المجموعة الرابعة مع الهلال السوداني، حوريا الغيني، والمغرب الفاسي، حيث يواجه المغرب الفاسي في الجولة الأولى. أما الأهلي، فقد وقع في المجموعة الأولى مع الرجاء المغربي، أول أغسطس الأنجولي، وإسكو كارا التوجولي، حيث يبدأ مبارياته بمواجهة أول أغسطس. ستنطلق المنافسات في نوفمبر 2026.

football.title: خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق - تاق برس
football.content: خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق — تاق برس اعجاب المتابعين الأحد, نوفمبر 1, 2026 من نحن السياسة التحريرية للإعلان على تاق برس اتصل بنا تاق برس - اخبار السودان والعالم الرئيسية أخبار عاجلة سياسية منوعات وثقافة إقتصاد رياضة علوم وتكنلوجيا مقالات أخري تقارير صحة الرئيسية أخبار رياضة خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق بواسطة editor في أكتوبر 31, 2026 178 مشاركة متابعات تاق برس – تتجه العلاقة بين الغاني كواسي أبياه، المدير الفني للمنتخب الوطني السوداني الأول، والاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم نحو منعطف بالغ الخطورة، في ظل تصاعد الضغوط والتدخلات التي باتت تحاصر المدرب، وتضع تجربته مع صقور الجديان على المحك، وسط مؤشرات متزايدة على اقتراب نهاية مشواره مع المنتخب. وتشير المعلومات التي تحصل عليها “الترا سودان” من داخل مجلس إدارة الاتحاد إلى أن أبياه بات يشعر بأن ما يتعرض له يمثل تحركات منظمة تستهدف تقويض صلاحياته وإضعاف موقفه، تمهيداً لإبعاده عن قيادة المنتخب. وهو ما أسرّ به لعدد من المقربين منه، معبّراً عن استيائه الشديد من الأجواء التي يعمل فيها. وبحسب المعلومات ذاتها، فإن المدرب الغاني بات يعتقد أن هناك مخططاً يُحاك ضده، وأن بعض القرارات والتوجهات الأخيرة داخل الاتحاد لا يمكن فصلها عن مساعٍ لإجباره على مغادرة موقعه، بعدما وجد نفسه في مواجهة تدخلات متكررة في صميم اختصاصاته الفنية. التغييرات التي طالت الجهازين الإداري والفني المساعد لم تكن أمراً عابراً بالنسبة للمدرب الغاني، خصوصاً بعد إبعاد المدير الإداري أبوبكر الماحي، وابتعاد المدرب العام صلاح الفنج عن موقعه ضمن المنظومة التي عملت معه خلال الفترة الماضية. ويمثل الرجلان عنصرين مهمين في منظومة أبياه، وكان المدرب ينظر إليهما باعتبارهما من ركائز الاستقرار داخل المنتخب، الأمر الذي دفعه إلى المطالبة بإعادة ترتيب الأوضاع بما يضمن عودة الانسجام إلى الجهازين الفني والإداري. لكن ما حدث عزز شعوره بأن هناك توجهاً لإعادة تشكيل المنظومة المحيطة به، دون اعتبار لرؤيته أو احتياجاته، وبكوادر لا تمتلك بالضرورة الخبرة المطلوبة للعمل في منتخب بحجم صقور الجديان. ومن أكثر الملفات التي أثارت غضب أبياه الضغوط المتواصلة بشأن إبعاد عدد من أصحاب الخبرة والعناصر الأساسية التي شكلت العمود الفقري للمنتخب خلال مشواره الأخير. فالمدرب الغاني لا يرى مبرراً للتخلي عن عناصر أثبتت جدارتها وقدمت الكثير للمنتخب، لمجرد ارتباط بعضها بملف المطالبة بالمستحقات المالية. كما لا يخفي تحفظاته على محاولات فرض أسماء جديدة ضمن القائمة، دون أن تكون هناك قناعة فنية مكتملة بشأن قدراتها. وتفاقمت الأزمة مع التوجه نحو تغيير نسبة من قوام المنتخب وإقحام عناصر من منتخب الشباب، في وقت يرى فيه أبياه أن الإحلال والتجديد لا ينبغي أن يتحولا إلى قرارات فوقية تتجاوز التقييم الفني واحتياجات المنتخب. ولم تتوقف مصادر الإحباط عند التدخل في اختيار اللاعبين وإدارة الجهاز الفني، بل امتدت إلى عدم تنفيذ عدد من البرامج الإعدادية التي اقترحها المدرب، وفي مقدمتها إقامة معسكر مبكر عقب فراغ الهلال والمريخ من مشاركتهما في البطولات الأفريقية. وكان أبياه يعوّل على الاستفادة من تلك الفترة في تجهيز المنتخب بصورة مثالية، والاستفادة من وجود العناصر الأساسية في السودان. غير أن عدم الاستجابة للمقترح أضاف حلقة جديدة إلى سلسلة الخلافات بينه والاتحاد. وبدا للمدرب أن برامجه وتصوراته لا تجد الاهتمام المطلوب، وأنه مطالب بتحقيق النتائج وتحمل المسؤولية كاملة، دون أن تتوفر له الظروف والصلاحيات اللازمة. التطور الأكثر إثارة في هذه الأزمة أن أبياه، وفقاً للمعلومات التي تحصلت عليها مصادرنا، لمح للمقربين منه بأن مواجهتي المنتخب أمام السنغال ذهاباً وإياباً قد تكونان آخر مشاويره مع صقور الجديان. وتشير هذه المعطيات إلى أن المدرب الغاني بدأ بالفعل التفكير في وضع حد لتجربته عقب المباراتين، في ظل قناعته بأن الأجواء الحالية لم تعد تساعده على مواصلة العمل بالصورة التي يريدها، وأن حجم التدخلات والضغوط تجاوز الحدود التي يمكن التعايش معها. وإذا مضى أبياه في هذا الاتجاه، فإن المنتخب الوطني سيكون أمام خسارة مدرب كبير قاده إلى مرحلة مميزة من النتائج والإنجازات، في وقت يحتاج فيه إلى الاستقرار والاستمرارية أكثر من حاجته إلى الدخول في مغامرة فنية وإدارية جديدة. ما يحدث الآن يتجاوز خلافاً حول قائمة أو لاعب أو معسكر إعدادي. نحن أمام أزمة ثقة تتسع يوماً بعد يوم، ومدرب بات يشعر بأنه مستهدف، وأن هناك من يعمل على إضعاف تجربته وإفقاده أدوات النجاح، قبل أن يصبح رحيله أمراً واقعاً. والسؤال الذي ينبغي أن يجيب عنه الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم ليس ما إذا كان أبياه سيغادر فحسب، بل من يتحمل مسؤولية الوصول بعلاقة المنتخب مع مدرب صنع معه إنجازات كبيرة إلى هذه المرحلة؟ هل هناك مشروع فني بديل يستحق التضحية بتجربة أبياه؟ أم أن صقور الجديان يدفعون ثمن صراعات وتدخلات إدارية لا علاقة لها بمصلحة المنتخب؟ المؤكد أن خسارة أبياه، إن حدثت
